hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? how often does your phone pull you away from what you’re doing?
options: same here, honestly. this one’s for us.
then you know the tug. listen.
that’s rare. here’s an old picture of what you’re doing.

steps.line: The Buddha once told his monks a story. A huge crowd gathers to watch the most beautiful girl in the land dance and sing.
steps.label: a story the Buddha told

steps.line: Then a man is handed a bowl of oil, filled to the very brim. He must carry it right between the crowd and the dancer.
steps.label: a story the Buddha told

steps.line: Behind him walks a guard with a drawn sword. If he spills even one drop, it will cost him his life.
steps.label: a story the Buddha told

steps.q: The Buddha tells this as a picture. What do you guess the brim-full bowl stands for?
o: Your life, which one slip can spill
Your attention to your own body
The teaching, carried with great care
steps.why: “The bowl full of oil stands for mindfulness directed to the body,” the Buddha says (SN 47.20). The crowd and the dancer are everything that pulls attention away.

steps.line: Would he look up at the dancer? No, said the monks. He would keep his mind on the bowl, one step after another.
steps.label: a story the Buddha told

steps.q: Why does the bowl have to be full to the brim?
o: Oil was costly in those days
So the guard can see it clearly
So that every single step needs his attention
steps.why: Half full, he could relax. Brim full, he has to keep coming back to it, step after step.

steps.line: “The bowl full of oil,” the Buddha said, “stands for mindfulness of the body.” His word was sati, from an old word for memory.

steps.q: Sati is usually translated “mindfulness.” When did that English word take on this job?
o: The 1880s, by a British scholar of Pali
The 1960s, with the first meditation teachers
steps.why: The choice is usually credited to the British Pali scholar T. W. Rhys Davids, around 1881. The English word was centuries old; he gave it a new job.

steps.line: Today, many people sit with meditation apps. Much of what they teach grew out of practices like this one.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Meditation apps often teach mindfulness on its own. In the Buddha’s teaching, what does it sit beside?
o: Kind speech, honest work and wise action
Fasting, chanting and giving up home
Calm breathing, good sleep and exercise
steps.why: Right mindfulness is the seventh part of the Noble Eightfold Path, alongside right speech, right action and right livelihood. It was never meant to stand alone.

say: so, is meditation buddhist? much of it grew from buddhist practice. but in the buddha’s teaching, mindfulness is one part of an eight-part path, next to how you speak, act and earn a living.
and no one has to become a buddhist to sit. the tradition’s own word for its teaching is an invitation: come and see.

steps.q: Why does “remembering” fit the man with the bowl better than just “paying attention”?
o: He has to recall the path he was shown
He keeps catching his drift and coming back
He keeps the guard’s warning in mind
steps.why: Attention slips; sati is noticing the slip and returning, step after step. That’s why teachers call it remembering, not straining.

today.say: pick one ordinary thing you’ll carry today: a cup of tea, a bag, the walk to your car. carry it the whole way like the bowl of oil. when your mind wanders, remember, and come back.
options: one walk with the bowl. that’s sati.
then you remember again. that’s the practice, not a failure.

sources: Janapadakalyani Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 47.20 (at Sedaka, among the Sumbhas): the crowd, the most beautiful girl of the land dancing and singing, the bowl of oil filled to the brim, the man with a drawn sword behind; the bowl as mindfulness
Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 56.11: right mindfulness as one of the eight factors of the path
Sati related to Sanskrit smrti, memory; “mindfulness” as T. W. Rhys Davids’ rendering
ehipassiko, “come and see,” in the recollection of the Dhamma (e.g. Anguttara Nikaya 11.12)
check: The teach, match and today steps speak of mindfulness in general; the sutta’s simile is specifically mindfulness directed to the body (the caption says so).
